title: Real Numbers and Limits of Sequences
text:
TipNatural number





The Peano axioms describe the arithmetic properties of the set of natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\). The formal definition is as follows:

There exists an element \(0 \in \mathbb{N}\).
There exists a function \[
S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}
\] called the successor function, such that for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(S(n)\) represents the next natural number after \(n\).
Zero is not the successor of any number \[
\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\; S(n) \neq 0
\]
Successor function is injective (one-to-one) \[
\forall m, n \in \mathbb{N},\; S(m) = S(n) \implies m = n
\]
Principle of mathematical induction. For any property \(P(n)\) defined on \(\mathbb{N}\): If \[
P(0) \text{ is true, and } \forall n \in \mathbb{N},\; P(n) \Rightarrow P(S(n)),
\]
then \[
\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\; P(n) \text{ is true.}
\]

Addition:
The addition \(+ : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) is defined recursively as follows:
\[
a + 0 = a
\]
\[
a + S(b) = S(a + b)
\]
Multiplication:
The multiplication \(\times : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) is defined recursively as follows:
\[
a \times 0 = 0
\]
\[
a \times S(b) = a \times b + a
\]
Order Relation:
For all \(m, n \in \mathbb{N}\):
\[
m < S(n) \iff (m < n) \text{ or } (m = n).
\]
This defines \(<\) recursively based on the successor structure.
Theorems:

\(a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c\).
\(a + 0 = 0 + a = a\).
\(a + b = b + a\).
\((a + b)\times c = a \times c + b \times c\).
\(a \times 1 = 1 \times a = a\).
\(a \times b = b \times a\).
\(a \times (b \times c) = (a \times b) \times c\).










TipInteger





Integers can be defined from natural numbers as equivalence classes of ordered pairs of natural numbers:
\[
\mathbb{Z} = \{ (a, b) \mid a, b \in \mathbb{N} \}
\] We define an equivalence relation:
\[
(a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff a + d = b + c
\]

Each equivalence class \([(a, b)]\) represents the difference between \(a\) and \(b\). Thus we have: \[
  \begin{aligned}
  0 &= [(0, 0)], \\
  1 &= [(1, 0)], \\
  -1 &= [(0, 1)], \\
  a - b &= [(a, b)].
  \end{aligned}
  \]

Addition:
\[
[(a, b)] + [(c, d)] = [(a + c,\, b + d)]
\]
Multiplication:
\[
[(a, b)] \times [(c, d)] = [(ac + bd,\, ad + bc)]
\]
These definitions are well-defined, meaning the result does not depend on the choice of representatives of the equivalence classes.
Order Relation:
\[
[(a,b)] < [(c,d)] \iff a + d < b + c.
\]
Theorems:

\(a + b = b + a, \qquad a \times b = b \times a\).
\(a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c, \qquad a \times (b \times c) = (a \times b) \times c\).
\(a + 0 = a, \qquad a \times 1 = a\).
\(\forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \; \exists (-a) \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ such that } a + (-a) = 0\).
\(a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c\).










TipRational Number





The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) is constructed from the integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) as the set of equivalence classes of ordered pairs of integers:
\[
\mathbb{Q} = \{ (a, b) \mid a \in \mathbb{Z},\; b \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\} \}
\]
Each pair \((a,b)\) intuitively represents the fraction \(\dfrac{a}{b}\).
We define an equivalence relation: \[
(a,b) \sim (c,d) \iff ad = bc
\]
Each equivalence class \([(a,b)]\) corresponds to a rational number. We write:
\[
\dfrac{a}{b} = [(a,b)], \quad \text{where } b \neq 0
\]
Addition:
\[
\dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad + bc}{bd}
\]
Multiplication:
\[
\dfrac{a}{b} \times \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}
\]
Additive Inverse:
\[
-\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{-a}{b}
\]
Multiplicative Inverse:
\[
\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{-1} = \dfrac{b}{a}, \quad a \neq 0
\]
Order relation:
To compare two rational numbers, let
\[
\dfrac{a}{b}, \; \dfrac{c}{d} \in \mathbb{Q}, \quad b > 0, \; d > 0.
\]
We define the order relation \(<\) on \(\mathbb{Q}\) by:
\[
\dfrac{a}{b} < \dfrac{c}{d} \iff ad < bc.
\]
Theorems:

\(a+b = b+a, \qquad a\times b = b\times a\).
\(a+(b+c) = (a+b)+c, \qquad a\times(b\times c) = (a\times b)\times c\).
\(a+0 = a, \qquad a\times1 = a\).
\(\forall a \in \mathbb{Q},\; \exists (-a) \text{ such that } a+(-a)=0\).
\(\forall a \in \mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\},\; \exists a^{-1} \text{ such that } a\times a^{-1}=1\).
\(a\times(b+c) = a\times b + a\times c\).










TipReal number





A Dedekind cut in \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a partition \((A, B)\) of \(\mathbb{Q}\) satisfying:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1)\quad & A, B \subset \mathbb{Q}, \; A \cup B = \mathbb{Q}, \; A \cap B = \varnothing, \\[4pt]
(2)\quad & \forall a \in A,\; \forall b \in B,\; a < b, \\[4pt]
(3)\quad & A \text{ has no greatest element.}
\end{aligned}
\] Each real number is identified with one such cut \(A\), which intuitively represents “all rationals less than that real number.”
The set of all Dedekind cuts is denoted by:
\[
\mathbb{R} = \{ A \subset \mathbb{Q} \mid A \text{ is a Dedekind cut} \}.
\]

For example:

\[
\sqrt{2} = \{ q \in \mathbb{Q} \mid q < 0 \text{ or } q^2 < 2 \}.
\]
Addition:
\[
A + B = \{ a + b \mid a \in A,\, b \in B \}.
\]
Multiplication:
(for positive cuts) \[
A \times B = \{ a \times b \mid a \in A,\, b \in B,\; a,b > 0 \}.
\]
Negatives and general cases are defined symmetrically by extending signs.
Order Relation:
Define: \[
A < B \iff A \subsetneq B.
\]
This relation extends the usual order on \(\mathbb{Q}\) and makes \((\mathbb{R}, <)\) a totally ordered set.
Theorems:

\(a+b = b+a, \qquad a\times b = b\times a\).
\(a+(b+c) = (a+b)+c, \qquad a\times(b\times c) = (a\times b)\times c\).
\(a+0 = a, \qquad a\times1 = a\).
\(\forall a \in \mathbb{Q},\; \exists (-a) \text{ such that } a+(-a)=0\).
\(\forall a \in \mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\},\; \exists a^{-1} \text{ such that } a\times a^{-1}=1\).
\(a\times(b+c) = a\times b + a\times c\).
The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) is dense in \(\mathbb{R}\):

\[
\forall a,b \in \mathbb{R},\; a < b \Rightarrow \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } a < r < b.
\]

title: Real Numbers and Limits of Sequences
text:
1.2 Sequences and Convergent Sequences






TipConvergent Sequence





Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence and \(a\) be a real number. If for any given \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an \(N \in \mathbb{N}^*\) such that whenever \(n > N\), we have: \[
|a_n - a| < \varepsilon
\]
then the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is said to have the limit \(a\) as \(n\) tends to infinity, denoted as: \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = a
\]
It can also be briefly denoted as \(a_n \to a\) (\(n \to \infty\)). We also say that the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges to \(a\). A sequence that has a limit is called a convergent sequence; a sequence that does not converge is called a divergent sequence.
Examples:

\(\alpha > 0\), \(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n^\alpha} = 0.\)
\(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} n^{1/n} = 1.\)





Theorem 1.1 If the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges, then it has only one limit. That is to say, the limit of a convergent sequence is unique.







TipBounded Sequence





Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence. If there exists a real number \(A\), such that \(a_n \leqslant A\) holds for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}^*\), then \(\{a_n\}\) is said to be bounded above, and \(A\) is an upper bound of this sequence.
Similarly, we can define a sequence that is bounded below.
If the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) has both a lower bound and an upper bound, then it is called a bounded sequence.




Theorem 1.2 Convergent sequences are bounded.







TipSubsequence





Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence, and let \(k_i \in \mathbb{N}^*\) (\(i=1, 2, 3, \dots\)) satisfy \(k_1 < k_2 < k_3 < \dots\). Then the sequence \(\{a_{k_n}\}\) is called a subsequence of \(\{a_n\}\).




Theorem 1.3 Let the limit of a convergent sequence \(\{a_n\}\) be \(a\). Then any subsequence of \(\{a_n\}\) also converges to \(a\).


Corollary 1.1 A necessary and sufficient condition for the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) to converge is that both its even subsequence \(\{a_{2n}\}\) and its odd subsequence \(\{a_{2n-1}\}\) converge, and have the same limit.


Theorem 1.4 Let \(\{a_n\}\) and \(\{b_n\}\) both be convergent sequences. Then \(\{a_n + b_n\}\) and \(\{a_n b_n\}\) are also convergent sequences. If \(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} b_n \neq 0\), then \(\{a_n / b_n\}\) is also convergent, and:
\(\text{(1)}\quad \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} (a_n \pm b_n) = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n \pm \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} b_n.\)
\(\text{(2)}\quad \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n b_n = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n \cdot \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} b_n.\)
\(\text{(3)}\quad \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \frac{\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n}{\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} b_n}, \quad \text{where } \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} b_n \neq 0.\)







TipInfinitesimal Sequence





If the limit of a convergent sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is equal to 0, then this sequence is called an infinitesimal sequence, or simply referred to as an infinitesimal.




Theorem 1.5 Let \[
a_n \leqslant b_n \leqslant c_n \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}^*)
\]
If \(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} c_n = a\), then \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n = a
\]
Examples:

\(a > 1, k \in \mathbb{N}^*\), \(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty}\frac{n^k}{a^n} = 0.\)
\(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+2}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+n}} = 1\).








TipInfinite Sequence





If the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) satisfies the condition: for any positive number \(A\), there exists an \(N \in \mathbb{N}^*\) such that whenever \(n > N\), we have \(a_n > A\), then the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is said to tend to \(+\infty\) (positive infinity), denoted as \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = +\infty.
\]
If for any positive number \(A\), there exists an \(N \in \mathbb{N}^*\) such that whenever \(n > N\), we have \(a_n < -A\), then the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is said to tend to \(-\infty\) (negative infinity), denoted as \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = -\infty.
\]
If \(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} |a_n| = +\infty\), then the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is said to tend to \(\infty\), denoted as \(\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = \infty\).
Regardless of which of the three cases \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = +\infty, \quad \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = -\infty, \quad \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = \infty
\] holds, the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is called infinity (or an infinite sequence).

title: Real Numbers and Limits of Sequences
text:
1.3 Monotonic Sequences






TipMonotonic Sequence





If the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) satisfies \[
a_n \leqslant a_{n+1} \quad (n = 1, 2, \dots),
\] then this sequence is called an increasing sequence; if \(\{a_n\}\) satisfies \[
a_n \geqslant a_{n+1} \quad (n = 1, 2, \dots),
\] then this sequence is called a decreasing sequence. If the above two inequalities are strict, i.e., \(a_n < a_{n+1}\) (or \(a_n > a_{n+1}\)) (\(n=1, 2, \dots\)), then this sequence is called strictly increasing (or strictly decreasing).
Increasing or decreasing sequences are collectively called monotonic sequences.




Theorem 1.6 A monotonic and bounded sequence must have a limit.


Theorem 1.7 For \(n \in \mathbb{N}^*\), let the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) be defined by: \[
a_n = 1 + \frac{1}{2^\alpha} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n^\alpha}
\]
where \(\alpha > 1\). Then the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is convergent.


Theorem 1.8 Let \(I_n = [a_n, b_n]\) (\(n \in \mathbb{N}^*\)), and let \[
I_1 \supset I_2 \supset I_3 \supset \cdots \supset I_n \supset I_{n+1} \supset \cdots.
\]
If the length of this sequence of intervals \(|I_n| = b_n - a_n \to 0\) (\(n \to \infty\)), then the intersection \[
\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} I_n
\] contains a unique point.

section: 1.4 The Base of Natural Logarithm e
text:
1.4 The Base of Natural Logarithm e






TipDefinition of e





Let two sequences be defined as \[
a_n = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n, \quad
b_n = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^{n+1}.
\]
Then:

\(a_n\) is monotonically increasing.
\(b_n\) is monotonically decreasing.
For all \(n\), \(a_n < b_n\).
Therefore, both sequences converge and have the same limit.

We define this common limit as
\[
e = \lim_{n \to +\infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n.
\]




Theorem 1.9 Let the sequence \(\{s_n\}\) be defined as: \[
s_n = 1 + \frac{1}{1!} + \frac{1}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n!} \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}^*).
\]
Then for any positive integer \(n\), the error in approximating the base of the natural logarithm \(e\) by \(s_n\) satisfies the following inequality: \[
0 < e - s_n \leqslant \frac{1}{n! n} \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}^*).
\]

section: 1.5 Fundamental Sequences and Cauchy Convergence Criterion
text:
1.5 Fundamental Sequences and Cauchy Convergence Criterion






TipCauchy Sequence





Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a real sequence. For any given \(\varepsilon > 0\), if there exists an \(N \in \mathbb{N}^*\) such that whenever \(m, n \in \mathbb{N}^*\) and \(m, n > N\), we have \[
| a_m - a_n | < \varepsilon,
\] then the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is called a fundamental sequence or a Cauchy sequence.




Lemma 1.1 Every sequence contains a monotonic subsequence.


Theorem 1.10 From any bounded sequence, a convergent subsequence can always be selected.


Theorem 1.11 A necessary and sufficient condition for a sequence to converge is that it is a fundamental sequence.

title: Real Numbers and Limits of Sequences
text:
1.6 Supremum and Infimum






TipSupremum





Let \(E\) be a non-empty set bounded above. A real number \(\beta\) satisfies the following two conditions:
\(\text{(1)}\quad\)For any \(x \in E\), we have \(x \leqslant \beta\);
\(\text{(2)}\quad\)For any given \(\varepsilon > 0\), there must exist an \(x_{\varepsilon} \in E\) such that \(x_{\varepsilon} > \beta - \varepsilon\).
In this case, \(\beta\) is called the supremum of the set \(E\), denoted as \(\beta = \sup E\).









TipInfimum





Let \(E\) be a non-empty set bounded below. A real number \(\alpha\) satisfies the following two conditions:
\(\text{(1)}\quad\)For any \(x \in E\), we have \(x \geqslant \alpha\);
\(\text{(2)}\quad\)For any given \(\varepsilon > 0\), there must exist a \(y_{\varepsilon} \in E\) such that \(y_{\varepsilon} < \alpha + \varepsilon\).
In this case, \(\alpha\) is called the infimum of the set \(E\), denoted as \(\alpha = \inf E\).




Theorem 1.12 A non-empty set bounded above must have a supremum; a non-empty set bounded below must have an infimum.


Theorem 1.13 Let \([a, b]\) be a finite closed interval, and let \(\{I_\lambda\}\) be an open cover of it. Then a finite number of members (open intervals) can necessarily be selected from this family of open intervals, such that the family formed by these finite open intervals is still an open cover of \([a, b]\).

title: Real Numbers and Limits of Sequences
text:
1.7 Limit Superior and Limit Inferior






TipLimit Superior and Limit Inferior





Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence, and let \(E\) be the set composed of all limit points of \(\{a_n\}\). Let \[
a^* = \sup E, \quad a_* = \inf E,
\] then \(a^*\) and \(a_*\) are called the limit superior and limit inferior of the sequence \(\{a_n\}\), respectively, denoted as \[
a^* = \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n, \quad a_* = \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n.
\]




Theorem 1.14 Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence. Then:
\(\text{(1)}\quad a^* \in E\);
\(\text{(2)}\quad\)If \(x > a^*\), then there exists an \(N \in \mathbb{N}^*\) such that whenever \(n \geqslant N\), we have \(a_n < x\);
\(\text{(3)}\quad a^*\) is the unique number satisfying the first two properties.


Theorem 1.15 For the sequence \(\{a_n\}\), define \(\alpha_n = \inf\limits_{k \geqslant n} a_k\) and \(\beta_n = \sup\limits_{k \geqslant n} a_k\). Then:
\(\text{(1)}\quad \{\alpha_n\}\) is an increasing sequence, and \(\{\beta_n\}\) is a decreasing sequence;
\(\text{(2)}\quad \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \alpha_n = a_*, \quad \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \beta_n = a^*\).


1.7.1 Stolz Theorem

Theorem 1.16 (\(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) Type) Let \(\{b_n\}\) be a strictly increasing sequence tending to \(+\infty\). If \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n - a_{n-1}}{b_n - b_{n-1}} = A,
\]
then \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = A,
\]
where \(A\) can be \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\).


Theorem 1.17 (\(\frac{0}{0}\) Type) Let \(\{a_n\}\) and \(\{b_n\}\) be two sequences converging to 0. If \(\{b_n\}\) is strictly decreasing and \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n - a_{n-1}}{b_n - b_{n-1}} = A,
\]
then \[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = A,
\]
where \(A\) can be a finite number, \(+\infty\), or \(-\infty\).

TipCardinality of Sets





Let \(\mathbb{N}^*\) be the set of all positive integers, and \[
N_n = \{1, 2, \cdots, n\}.
\]
\(\text{(1)}\quad\)If there exists a positive integer \(n\) such that set \(A \sim N_n\), then \(A\) is called a finite set. The empty set is also considered a finite set.
\(\text{(2)}\quad\)If set \(A\) is not a finite set, then \(A\) is called an infinite set.
\(\text{(3)}\quad\)If \(A \sim \mathbb{N}^*\), then \(A\) is called a countable set.
\(\text{(4)}\quad\)If \(A\) is neither a finite set nor a countable set, then \(A\) is called an uncountable set.
\(\text{(5)}\quad\)If \(A\) is a finite set or \(A\) is a countable set, then \(A\) is called at most countable.




Theorem 2.1 Every infinite subset of a countable set \(A\) is a countable set.


Theorem 2.2 Let \(\{E_n\}\) (\(n=1, 2, 3, \cdots\)) be a sequence of at most countable sets. Let \[
S = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} E_n,
\] then \(S\) is an at most countable set.

title: Continuity of Functions
text:
2.3 Limit of Functions






TipLimits of Function





A real number \(x_0\) is called an accumulation point (or limit point) of a set \(I \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) if:
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists x \in I \text{ such that } 0 < |x - x_0| < \varepsilon.
\]
Let \(f : I \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(x_0\) be an accumulation point of \(I\). We say that the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(x_0\) is \(A \in \mathbb{R}\), written as \[
\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = A.
\]
if and only if
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists \delta > 0 \text{ such that } \forall x \in I,\;
0 < |x - x_0| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - A| < \varepsilon.
\]

The right-hand limit of a function \(f\) at \(x_0\) is denoted by \[
  \lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x) = A,
  \] which means: \[
  \forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists \delta > 0 \text{ such that } \forall x \in I,\; x_0 < x < x_0 + \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - A| < \varepsilon.
  \]
Similarly, the left-hand limit is defined by \[
  \lim_{x \to x_0^-} f(x) = A.
  \]





Theorem 2.3 A necessary and sufficient condition for the function \(f\) to have a limit \(l\) at \(x_0\) is that, for any sequence \(\{x_n \neq x_0 : n=1, 2, 3, \cdots\}\) converging to \(x_0\), the sequence \(\{f(x_n)\}\) has a limit \(l\).


Theorem 2.4 Let \(\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x)\) and \(\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} g(x)\) exist. Then:
\(\text{(1)}\quad\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} (f \pm g)(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x) \pm \lim\limits_{x \to x_0} g(x)\);
\(\text{(2)}\quad\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} fg(x) = \lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x) \cdot \lim\limits_{x \to x_0} g(x)\);
\(\text{(3)}\quad\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} \frac{f}{g}(x) = \frac{\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x)}{\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} g(x)}\), where \(\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} g(x) \neq 0\).







TipNeighborhood and Deleted Neighborhood





\[
B_\delta(x_0) = \{x : |x - x_0| < \delta\}, \quad B_\delta(\mathring{x}_0) = \{x : 0 < |x - x_0| < \delta\}.
\]
We call \(B_\delta(x_0)\) the neighborhood of \(x_0\) centered at \(x_0\) with radius \(\delta\) (abbreviated as the neighborhood of \(x_0\)), and \(B_\delta(\mathring{x}_0)\) the deleted neighborhood of \(x_0\) centered at \(x_0\) with radius \(\delta\) (abbreviated as the deleted neighborhood of \(x_0\)).




Theorem 2.5 A necessary and sufficient condition for the function \(f\) to have a limit at \(x_0\) is that for any given \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that for any \(x_1, x_2 \in B_\delta(\mathring{x}_0)\), we have \(|f(x_1) - f(x_2)| < \varepsilon\).


Theorem 2.6 Let \(\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x) = l\) and \(\lim\limits_{t \to t_0} g(t) = x_0\). If in some neighborhood \(B_{\eta}(t_0)\) of \(t_0\), \(g(t) \neq x_0\), then \[
\lim_{t \to t_0} f(g(t)) = l.
\]

2.4 Infinite Limits of Functions






TipLimit at Infinity





\[
\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = A
\]
means that
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists M > 0 \text{ such that } \forall x \in I,\; x > M \Rightarrow |f(x) - A| < \varepsilon.
\]
Similarly, \[
\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = A
\]
means
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists M > 0 \text{ such that } \forall x \in I,\; x < -M \Rightarrow |f(x) - A| < \varepsilon.
\]
\[
\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = A
\]
means
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists M > 0 \text{ such that } \forall x \in I,\; |x| > M \Rightarrow |f(x) - A| < \varepsilon.
\]









TipDefinition





Let \(c\) be one of \(x_0,\; x_0^+,\; x_0^-,\; -\infty,\; +\infty,\; \infty\). The neighborhood and deleted neighborhood of \(c\) are defined as follows:

TipGeneral Definition of Limit





Let \(c\) be one of \(x_0,\; x_0^+,\; x_0^-,\; -\infty,\; +\infty,\; \infty\), and let \(A\) be a real number or one of \(-\infty,\; +\infty,\; \infty\). We say that \(\lim\limits_{x \to c} f(x) = A\) iff:
For every neighborhood \(V\) of \(A\), there exists a deleted neighborhood \(W\) of \(c\) such that for all \(x \in I \cap W\), we have \(f(x) \in V\).









TipInfinite Quantity





When \(x \to c\), if \(f(x)\) grows without bound, we say \(f(x)\) is an infinite quantity (or positive/negative infinite quantity).
If \[
\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \infty
\quad \text{(i.e. } \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty \text{ or } \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = -\infty \text{)},
\] then \(f(x)\) diverges to infinity as \(x\) approaches \(c\).




Theorem 2.7 \[
\lim_{x \to \infty} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{x} \right)^x = e.
\]

title: Continuity of Functions
text:
2.5 Big O and Small o






TipBig O





When \(x \to c\), if \(f(x) = O(g(x))\), it means:
There exists \(M > 0\) and a deleted neighborhood \(W\) of \(c\) such that for all \(x \in I \cap W\), we have \(|f(x)| \le M |g(x)|\).

If \(f_1 = O(g)\) and \(f_2 = O(g)\) as \(x \to c\), then \(f_1 + f_2 = O(g).\)
If \(f_1 = O(g_1)\) and \(f_2 = O(g_2)\) as \(x \to c\), then \(f_1 f_2 = O(g_1 g_2).\)










TipSame Order





When \(x \to c\), if \(f\) and \(g\) are of the same order, denoted \(f = \Theta(g), \quad x \to c,\) it means:
\[
f = O(g) \text{ and } g = O(f),
\]
that is, there exist \(M > 0\) and a deleted neighborhood \(W\) of \(c\) such that for all \(x \in W\), \[
\frac{1}{M} |g(x)| \le |f(x)| \le M |g(x)|.
\]









TipSmall o





When \(x \to c\), if \(f(x) = o(g(x))\), it means:
For every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a deleted neighborhood \(W\) of \(c\) such that for all \(x \in W\), \[
|f(x)| \le \varepsilon |g(x)|.
\]

If \(f_1 = o(g)\) and \(f_2 = o(g)\) as \(x \to c\), then \(f_1 + f_2 = o(g).\)
If \(f_1 = o(g_1)\) and \(f_2 = O(g_2)\) as \(x \to c\), then \(f_1 f_2 = o(g_1 g_2).\)










TipAsymptotic Equivalence





When \(x \to c\), functions \(f\) and \(g\) are said to be asymptotically equivalent, written as \(f \sim g\), if \[
f = g + o(g).
\]
That is, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a deleted neighborhood \(W\) of \(c\) such that for all \(x \in W\), \[
|f(x) - g(x)| \le \varepsilon |g(x)|.
\]




Theorem 2.8 If \(x \to c\), and \(f + o(f) = G + o(g), \quad G = O(g),\) then \(f = G + o(g)\).


Corollary 2.1 If \(x \to c\), and \(f\) is equivalent to \(g\), then \(g\) is equivalent to \(f\).


Corollary 2.2 If \(x \to c\), and \(f\) is equivalent to \(g\), and \(g\) is equivalent to \(h\), then \(f\) is equivalent to \(h\).

title: Continuity of Functions
text:
2.6 Continuous Functions






TipContinuous Function





Let \(f: [a, b] \to \mathbf{R}\). We say that the function \(f\) is continuous at the point \(x_0 \in (a, b)\) if \[
\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0).
\]
That is to say, for any given \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a suitable \(\delta > 0\), such that when \(|x - x_0| < \delta\), we have \[
|f(x) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon.
\]

We say that \(f\) is right-continuous at \(x_0\) if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists \delta > 0\) such that for all \(x \in I\).

\[
x_0 \le x < x_0 + \delta \;\Rightarrow\; |f(x) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon.
\]

Similarly, \(f\) is left-continuous at \(x_0\) if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists \delta > 0\) such that for all \(x \in I\).

\[
x_0 - \delta < x \le x_0 \;\Rightarrow\; |f(x) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon.
\]
\[
f \text{ is continuous at } x_0
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
f \text{ is both right-continuous and left-continuous at } x_0.
\]




Theorem 2.9 If both \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(x_0\), then \[
f \pm g \text{ and } f g \text{ are continuous at } x_0.
\]
Moreover, if \(g(x_0) \neq 0\), then
\[
\dfrac{f}{g} \text{ is continuous at } x_0.
\]


Theorem 2.10 Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions such that: \[
\begin{cases}
f \text{ is continuous at } x_0, \\
g \text{ is continuous at } y_0 = f(x_0),
\end{cases}
\] then the composite function \(g \circ f\) is continuous at \(x_0\).


Theorem 2.11 Let \(I, J \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be intervals, and let \(f: I \to J\) be monotone and onto. Then \(f\) is a continuous function.







TipRemovable Discontinuity





A point \(x_0\) is called a removable discontinuity of a function \(f\) if:
\(\text{(1)}\quad x_0\) is a limit point of the domain \(I\) of \(f\), and the limit \[
\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)
\] exists;
\(\text{(2)}\quad f\) is either undefined at \(x_0\), or \[
f(x_0) \ne \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x).
\]

In other words, \(f\) is not continuous at \(x_0\), but it can be made continuous by appropriately redefining the value \(f(x_0)\).










TipJump Discontinuity





A point \(x_0\) is called a jump discontinuity if both one-sided limits exist but are not equal: \[
\lim_{x \to x_0^-} f(x) \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x).
\]









TipClassification






Type I discontinuities: include both removable and jump discontinuities.
Type II discontinuities: all other discontinuities that do not fall into the above categories.

title: Continuity of Functions
text:
2.7 Uniform Continuity of Functions






TipUniform Continuity





A function \(f\) is said to be uniformly continuous on a set \(K\), if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta_\varepsilon > 0\) such that
\[
\forall x, y \in K, \quad |x - y| < \delta_\varepsilon \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon.
\]

The function \(f\) is not uniformly continuous on a set \(K\) if and only if there exists an \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\) such that for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}^*\), one can find two points in \(K\), denoted as \(s_n\) and \(t_n\), such that although \(|s_n - t_n| < 1/n\), we have \[
  |f(s_n) - f(t_n)| \geqslant \varepsilon_0.
  \]

title: Continuity of Functions
section: 2.8 Properties of Continuous Functions on Bounded Closed Intervals
text:
2.8 Properties of Continuous Functions on Bounded Closed Intervals

Theorem 2.12 Let the function \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\), then \(f\) must be uniformly continuous on \([a, b]\).


Theorem 2.13 A continuous function on a bounded closed interval must be bounded on that interval.


Theorem 2.14 Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\). Let \[
M = \sup_{x \in [a, b]} f(x), \quad m = \inf_{x \in [a, b]} f(x),
\] then there must exist \(x^*, x_* \in [a, b]\), such that \[
f(x^*) = M, \quad f(x_*) = m.
\]


Theorem 2.15 If \(f\) is continuous on the interval \([a,b]\) and \(f(a) \ne f(b)\), then every real number between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) is attained as a function value of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).

title: Definite Integral
text:
TipDarboux Integral





Consider a bounded function \(f\) on a closed interval \([a,b]\), and a partition of \([a,b]\): \[
P: \quad a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b.
\]
For each subinterval \([x_{k-1}, x_k]\), define
\[
M_k = \sup_{x \in [x_{k-1},x_k]} f(x),
\qquad
m_k = \inf_{x \in [x_{k-1},x_k]} f(x).
\]
The upper Darboux sum of \(f\) with respect to the partition \(P\) is
\[
\overline{S}(f,P)
= \sum_{k=1}^{N} M_k (x_k - x_{k-1}),
\]
and the lower Darboux sum is
\[
\underline{S}(f,P)
= \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_k (x_k - x_{k-1}).
\]
Define \[
\underline{S}(f) = \sup_P\, \underline{S}(f,P), \qquad
\overline{S}(f) = \inf_P\, \overline{S}(f,P),
\]
where the supremum and infimum are taken over all partitions \(P\) of \([a,b]\).

\(\underline{S}(f)\) is called the Darboux lower integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\);
\(\overline{S}(f)\) is called the Darboux upper integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).

If \[
\underline{S}(f) = \overline{S}(f),
\] then \(f\) is said to be Darboux integrable on \([a,b]\). The common value is denoted by \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,
\] and is called the Darboux integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).




Theorem 5.1 For any two partitions \(P, Q\) of the interval \([a,b]\), let \(P \lor Q\) denote the partition consisting of all points in \(P \cup Q\). We call \(P \lor Q\) the common refinement of \(P\) and \(Q\). Then \[
\underline{S}(f, Q) \;\le\; \underline{S}(f, P \lor Q) \;\le\; \overline{S}(f, P \lor Q) \;\le\; \overline{S}(f, P).
\]


Theorem 5.2 A bounded function \(f\) on the closed interval \([a,b]\) is Darboux integrable if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) such that \[
\overline{S}(f,P) - \underline{S}(f,P) < \varepsilon.
\]


Theorem 5.3 A bounded function \(f\) on the closed interval \([a,b]\) is Darboux integrable, and \(I \in \mathbb{R}\) is its Darboux integral, if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) such that \[
I - \varepsilon < \underline{S}(f,P) \le I \le \overline{S}(f,P) < I + \varepsilon.
\]


Theorem 5.4 Every monotonic function on a bounded closed interval \([a,b]\) is Darboux integrable. More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for any partition \[
a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b,
\] if \[
\|P\| := \max_{1 \le k \le N} (x_k - x_{k-1}) < \delta,
\] then \[
\overline{S}(f,P) - \underline{S}(f,P) < \varepsilon .
\]


Theorem 5.5 If \(f\) is a bounded function on the closed interval \([a,b]\), and \(f\) is continuous on the open interval \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is Darboux integrable on \([a,b]\). More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for any partition \(P: a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b\),
if \[
\|P\| := \max_{1 \le k \le N} (x_k - x_{k-1}) < \delta,
\] then
\[
\overline{S}(f, P) - \underline{S}(f, P) < \varepsilon.
\]


Corollary 5.1 If a bounded function \(f\) on the closed interval \([a,b]\) has only finitely many discontinuities, then \(f\) is Darboux integrable on \([a,b]\).







TipRiemann Integral





For a function \(f:[a,b]\to \mathbb{R}\), a partition of the interval \([a,b]\) is \[
P:\ a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b.
\]
Along with a set of sample points \[
\xi = \{\xi_i\}_{i=1}^{N}, \qquad (\xi_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]),
\] the Riemann sum is defined as \[
S(f, P, \xi) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(\xi_i)(x_i - x_{i-1}).
\] A function \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is said to be Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\) if there exists a real number \(I \in \mathbb{R}\) such that for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) with the property that for any tagged partition \((P,\xi)\) of \([a,b]\), if the norm of the partition satisfies \(\|P\| < \delta\), then
\[
\left| S(f, P, \xi) - I \right| < \varepsilon.
\]
In this case, we call \(I\) the Riemann integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\), and write
\[
I = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx.
\]




Theorem 5.6 For a function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\), the following statements are equivalent:
\(\text{(1)}\quad f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\);
\(\text{(2)}\quad f\) is bounded on \([a,b]\), and Darboux integrable;
\(\text{(3)}\quad f\) is bounded on \([a,b]\), and the set of all discontinuities of \(f\) in \([a,b]\) forms a set of measure zero.

title: Definite Integral
text:
TipDarboux Integral





Consider a bounded function \(f\) on a closed interval \([a,b]\), and a partition of \([a,b]\): \[
P: \quad a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b.
\]
For each subinterval \([x_{k-1}, x_k]\), define
\[
M_k = \sup_{x \in [x_{k-1},x_k]} f(x),
\qquad
m_k = \inf_{x \in [x_{k-1},x_k]} f(x).
\]
The upper Darboux sum of \(f\) with respect to the partition \(P\) is
\[
\overline{S}(f,P)
= \sum_{k=1}^{N} M_k (x_k - x_{k-1}),
\]
and the lower Darboux sum is
\[
\underline{S}(f,P)
= \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_k (x_k - x_{k-1}).
\]
Define \[
\underline{S}(f) = \sup_P\, \underline{S}(f,P), \qquad
\overline{S}(f) = \inf_P\, \overline{S}(f,P),
\]
where the supremum and infimum are taken over all partitions \(P\) of \([a,b]\).

\(\underline{S}(f)\) is called the Darboux lower integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\);
\(\overline{S}(f)\) is called the Darboux upper integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).

If \[
\underline{S}(f) = \overline{S}(f),
\] then \(f\) is said to be Darboux integrable on \([a,b]\). The common value is denoted by \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,
\] and is called the Darboux integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).




Theorem 5.1 For any two partitions \(P, Q\) of the interval \([a,b]\), let \(P \lor Q\) denote the partition consisting of all points in \(P \cup Q\). We call \(P \lor Q\) the common refinement of \(P\) and \(Q\). Then \[
\underline{S}(f, Q) \;\le\; \underline{S}(f, P \lor Q) \;\le\; \overline{S}(f, P \lor Q) \;\le\; \overline{S}(f, P).
\]


Theorem 5.2 A bounded function \(f\) on the closed interval \([a,b]\) is Darboux integrable if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) such that \[
\overline{S}(f,P) - \underline{S}(f,P) < \varepsilon.
\]


Theorem 5.3 A bounded function \(f\) on the closed interval \([a,b]\) is Darboux integrable, and \(I \in \mathbb{R}\) is its Darboux integral, if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) such that \[
I - \varepsilon < \underline{S}(f,P) \le I \le \overline{S}(f,P) < I + \varepsilon.
\]


Theorem 5.4 Every monotonic function on a bounded closed interval \([a,b]\) is Darboux integrable. More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for any partition \[
a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b,
\] if \[
\|P\| := \max_{1 \le k \le N} (x_k - x_{k-1}) < \delta,
\] then \[
\overline{S}(f,P) - \underline{S}(f,P) < \varepsilon .
\]


Theorem 5.5 If \(f\) is a bounded function on the closed interval \([a,b]\), and \(f\) is continuous on the open interval \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is Darboux integrable on \([a,b]\). More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for any partition \(P: a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b\),
if \[
\|P\| := \max_{1 \le k \le N} (x_k - x_{k-1}) < \delta,
\] then
\[
\overline{S}(f, P) - \underline{S}(f, P) < \varepsilon.
\]


Corollary 5.1 If a bounded function \(f\) on the closed interval \([a,b]\) has only finitely many discontinuities, then \(f\) is Darboux integrable on \([a,b]\).







TipRiemann Integral





For a function \(f:[a,b]\to \mathbb{R}\), a partition of the interval \([a,b]\) is \[
P:\ a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_N = b.
\]
Along with a set of sample points \[
\xi = \{\xi_i\}_{i=1}^{N}, \qquad (\xi_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]),
\] the Riemann sum is defined as \[
S(f, P, \xi) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} f(\xi_i)(x_i - x_{i-1}).
\] A function \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is said to be Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\) if there exists a real number \(I \in \mathbb{R}\) such that for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) with the property that for any tagged partition \((P,\xi)\) of \([a,b]\), if the norm of the partition satisfies \(\|P\| < \delta\), then
\[
\left| S(f, P, \xi) - I \right| < \varepsilon.
\]
In this case, we call \(I\) the Riemann integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\), and write
\[
I = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx.
\]




Theorem 5.6 For a function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\), the following statements are equivalent:
\(\text{(1)}\quad f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\);
\(\text{(2)}\quad f\) is bounded on \([a,b]\), and Darboux integrable;
\(\text{(3)}\quad f\) is bounded on \([a,b]\), and the set of all discontinuities of \(f\) in \([a,b]\) forms a set of measure zero.

title: Definite Integral
section: 5.2 Properties and Computation of Definite Integrals
text:
5.2 Properties and Computation of Definite Integrals

Theorem 5.7 (Newton-Leibniz Formula) If \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) and \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\), then \[
\int_a^b f(u)\,du = F(b) - F(a).
\]


Theorem 5.8 If \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\) and on \([b,c]\), then \(f\) is integrable on \([a,c]\), and \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_b^c f(x)\,dx
= \int_a^c f(x)\,dx.
\]


Theorem 5.9 Assume \(f \in \mathcal{C}[a,b]\), \(g \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\), and \(g(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in [a,b]\). Then there exists \(\xi \in [a,b]\) such that \[
\int_a^b f(x)g(x)\,dx
= f(\xi)\int_a^b g(x)\,dx.
\]


Theorem 5.10 Assume that \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\). Define \[
F(x) = \int_a^x f(u)\,du.
\] Then \(F \in \mathcal{C}[a,b]\). Then
\(\text{(1)}\quad\)Then the integral with variable upper limit \(F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) \mathrm{d}t\) is continuous on \([a, b]\).
\(\text{(2)}\quad\)Let function \(f\) be continuous at a point \(x_0 \in [a, b]\). Then \(F\) is differentiable at \(x_0\), and \(F'(x_0) = f(x_0).\)


Theorem 5.11 Let function \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\). Then \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} \int_a^x f(t) \mathrm{d}t = f(x) \quad (a \leqslant x \leqslant b).
\]


Theorem 5.12 Let \(f, g \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\). Then \[
\left|
\int_a^b f(x)g(x)\,dx
\right|
\,\le\,
\sqrt{\int_a^b |f(x)|^2\,dx}\;
\sqrt{\int_a^b |g(x)|^2\,dx}.
\]


Theorem 5.13 If \(f^{(n+1)} \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\), then for every \(x \in [a,b]\), \[
f(x)
=
f(a)
+
f'(a)(x-a)
+
\cdots
+
\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n
+
\int_{a}^{x}
\frac{f^{(n+1)}(t)}{n!} (x - t)^n \, dt.
\]


Theorem 5.14 Suppose that \(f\) is continuous on an interval \(I\), \(a, b \in I\), and \(\varphi : [\alpha, \beta] \to I\) satisfies \(\varphi(\alpha) = a\), \(\varphi(\beta) = b\), and \(\varphi' \in \mathcal{R}[\alpha, \beta]\). Then \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
= \int_\alpha^\beta f(\varphi(t))\, \varphi'(t)\, dt.
\]

title: Definite Integral
text:
5.3 Improper Integrals






TipImproper Integral





Let \(f:[a,+\infty)\to \mathbb{R}\) be Riemann integrable on every bounded closed interval \([a,A]\).
If
\[
\lim_{A\to+\infty} \int_a^A f(x)\,dx
\]
exists, then the improper integral \(\displaystyle \int_a^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx\) is said to converge, and we define
\[
\int_a^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx
=
\lim_{A\to+\infty} \int_a^A f(x)\,dx.
\]
If the limit does not exist, the improper integral is said to diverge.
Similarly, we define \[
\int_{-\infty}^a g(x)\,dx
=
\lim_{A\to-\infty} \int_A^a g(x)\,dx.
\]
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be Riemann integrable on every bounded closed interval \([a,b]\).
If both improper integrals
\[
\int_a^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\int_{-\infty}^{a} f(x)\,dx
\]
converge, then the improper integral
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx
\]
is said to converge, and we define
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx
=
\int_{-\infty}^{a} f(x)\,dx
+
\int_{a}^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx.
\]
Let \(f:[a,b)\to\mathbb{R}\) be unbounded, but Riemann integrable on every bounded closed interval \([a,b-\delta]\) for \(\delta>0\). In this case, the integral \(\displaystyle \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) is called an improper integral, and \(b\) is called an improper point.
If
\[
\lim_{\delta\to 0^+} \int_a^{\,b-\delta} f(x)\,dx
\]
exists, then the improper integral \(\displaystyle \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) is said to converge, and we define
\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=
\lim_{\delta\to 0^+} \int_a^{\,b-\delta} f(x)\,dx.
\]
Similarly, one may define improper integrals where the left endpoint is an improper point.



Examples

\[
  \int_{1}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{x^p} \mathrm{d}x
  \]
Solution: \[
  \int_{1}^{A} \frac{1}{x^p} \mathrm{d}x =
  \begin{cases}
  \frac{1 - A^{1-p}}{p-1}, & p \neq 1, \\
  \ln A, & p = 1.
  \end{cases}
  \]
Therefore, the integral converges if and only if \(p > 1\). When it converges, the limit is:
\[
  \int_{1}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{x^p} \mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{p-1}
  \]
\[
  \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x^p} \mathrm{d}x
  \]
Solution: \[
  \int_{\delta}^{1} \frac{1}{x^p} \mathrm{d}x =
  \begin{cases}
  \frac{1 - \delta^{1-p}}{1-p}, & p \neq 1, \\
  -\ln \delta, & p = 1.
  \end{cases}
  \]
Therefore, the integral converges if and only if \(p < 1\). When it converges, the limit is:
\[
  \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x^p} \mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{1-p}
  \]


Theorem 5.15 Suppose \(\int_{a}^{\omega} f'(x)g(x) \mathrm{d}x\) converges and \(\lim\limits_{x \to \omega^-} f(x)g(x)\) converges. Then \(\int_{a}^{\omega} f(x)g'(x) \mathrm{d}x\) converges, and: \[
\int_{a}^{\omega} f(x)g'(x) \mathrm{d}x = f(x)g(x) \bigg|_{a}^{\omega} - \int_{a}^{\omega} f'(x)g(x) \mathrm{d}x.
\]


Theorem 5.16 The improper integral \(\int_{a}^{+\infty} f(x) \mathrm{d}x\) converges if and only if for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(N_{\varepsilon} > 0\) such that for any \(A_2 > A_1 > N_{\varepsilon}\), the following holds: \[
\left| \int_{A_1}^{A_2} f(x) \mathrm{d}x \right| < \varepsilon.
\]







TipAbsolutely Convergent





An improper integral \(\int_{a}^{+\infty} f(x) \mathrm{d}x\) is said to be absolutely convergent, or \(f\) is absolutely integrable on the interval \([a, +\infty)\), if the improper integral \(\int_{a}^{+\infty} |f(x)| \mathrm{d}x\) converges.
From the inequality:
\[
\left| \int_{A_1}^{A_2} f(x) \mathrm{d}x \right| \leq \int_{A_1}^{A_2} |f(x)| \mathrm{d}x
\]
It is known that any absolutely convergent improper integral is also convergent.









TipDefinition





An improper integral is said to be conditionally convergent if it converges but is not absolutely convergent.




Theorem 5.17 Let \(f\) be Riemann integrable on any bounded closed interval \([a, A]\), and let \(g\) be monotonic. If:

\(\int_{a}^{A} f(x) \mathrm{d}x\) is bounded for all \(A > a\),
\(\lim\limits_{x \to +\infty} g(x) = 0\),

then the improper integral \(\int_{a}^{+\infty} f(x)g(x) \mathrm{d}x\) converges.


Theorem 5.18 Let \(f\) be Riemann integrable on any bounded closed interval \([a, A]\), and let \(g\) be monotonic. If:

The improper integral \(\int_{a}^{+\infty} f(x) \mathrm{d}x\) converges,
\(g(x)\) is bounded on the interval \([a, +\infty)\),

then the improper integral \(\int_{a}^{+\infty} f(x)g(x) \mathrm{d}x\) converges.

title: Definite Integral
text:
5.4 Applications of Definite Integrals






TipThe Gamma Function





For any \(\alpha > 0\):
\[
\Gamma(\alpha) = \int_{0}^{+\infty} x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x} \mathrm{d}x
\]
The function satisfies \(\Gamma(\alpha+1) = \alpha\Gamma(\alpha)\) and \(\Gamma(1) = 1\). Therefore, for any positive integer \(n\):
\[
\Gamma(n+1) = n!
\]









TipThe Beta Function





For any \(\alpha > 0, \beta > 0\):
\[
B(\alpha, \beta) = \int_{0}^{1} x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1} \mathrm{d}x
\]
It satisfies \(B(\alpha+1, \beta) = \frac{\alpha}{\beta} B(\alpha, \beta+1)\).

The relationship between the Beta function and the Gamma function is given by the following identity:

\[
B(\alpha, \beta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}
\]









TipThe area of a Plane Region





Area formula for a simple closed parametric curve
For a curve given by \(\gamma: x = x(t),\, y = y(t),\, \alpha \le t \le \beta\), the area enclosed by \(\gamma\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area}
&= - \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} y(t)\, x'(t)\, dt
   = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} x(t)\, y'(t)\, dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
Averaging these two expressions yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area}
&= \frac{1}{2} \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}
\bigl( x(t) y'(t) - x'(t) y(t) \bigr)\, dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently, using the determinant notation,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area}
&= \frac{1}{2}
\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}
\begin{vmatrix}
x(t) & x'(t) \\
y(t) & y'(t)
\end{vmatrix}
dt.
\end{aligned}
\]









TipLength of a Curve





Let \(\mathbf{x}(t) = (x_1(t), \dots, x_n(t)) \in \mathbb{R}^n\) be a parametrization of the curve \(\gamma\), where \(\alpha \le t \le \beta\). A partition of the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\) is given by
\[
\mathcal{P} : \alpha = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = \beta.
\]
For points on the curve defined by
\[
P_k = \mathbf{x}(t_k),
\]
the length of the polygonal line \(P_0 P_1 \cdots P_n\) is
\[
L(\mathcal{P})
=
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \| P_{k-1} P_k \|
=
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \| \mathbf{x}(t_k) - \mathbf{x}(t_{k-1}) \|.
\]
In coordinates, this becomes
\[
L(\mathcal{P})
=
\sum_{k=1}^{n}
\sqrt{
\bigl( x_1(t_k) - x_1(t_{k-1}) \bigr)^2
+ \cdots +
\bigl( x_n(t_k) - x_n(t_{k-1}) \bigr)^2 }.
\]
It is clear that as the partition is refined, the quantity \(L(\mathcal{P})\) increases.
If the supremum \(\displaystyle \sup_{\mathcal{P}} L(\mathcal{P})\) exists, then the curve \(\gamma\) is said to be rectifiable, and
\[
L(\gamma) = \sup_{\mathcal{P}} L(\mathcal{P})
\]
is called the length of the curve \(\gamma\). \[
L(\gamma) = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \| \mathbf{x}'(t) \| \, dt.
\]









TipCurvature and Torsion of a Curve





\[
l = l(t) = \int_{\alpha}^{t} \|\mathbf{x}'(s)\|\, ds
\]
\[
l'(t) = \|\mathbf{x}'(t)\| > 0
\]
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(l) = \mathbf{x}(t(l))
\quad \text{(the reparametrization by arc length)}
\]
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}'(l)
= \mathbf{x}'(t(l))\, t'(l)
= \frac{\mathbf{x}'(t)}{l'(t)}
= \frac{\mathbf{x}'(t)}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|}
\quad \text{is the unit tangent vector}
\]
\[
\sin\frac{\Delta \theta}{2}
= \frac{1}{2}\, \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}'(l+\Delta l) - \tilde{\mathbf{x}}'(l)\|
\]
\[
= \frac{1}{2}\, \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\,\Delta l + o(\Delta l)\|
\]
\[
= \frac{1}{2}\, \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\|\,|\Delta l| + o(\Delta l)
\]
\[
\Delta \theta
= \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\|\,\Delta l + o(\Delta l)
\]
\[
\lim_{\Delta l \to 0} \frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta l}
= \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\|
\]
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)
= \frac{d^2}{dl^2}\mathbf{x}(t(l))
= \frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{x}(t)\, \frac{dt}{dl} \right)\frac{dt}{dl}
\]
\[
= \left( \frac{\mathbf{x}'(t)}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|} \right)' \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|}
\]
\[
= \left(
\frac{\mathbf{x}''(t)}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|}
-
\frac{1}{2}\, \frac{\mathbf{x}'(t)\, 2\langle \mathbf{x}'(t),\mathbf{x}''(t)\rangle}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|^3}
\right)
\frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|}
\]
\[
=
\left(
\mathbf{x}''(t)
-
\frac{\mathbf{x}'(t)}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|}
\left\langle
\frac{\mathbf{x}'(t)}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|},
\mathbf{x}''(t)
\right\rangle
\right)
\frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}'(t)\|^2}
\]
\[
\lim_{\Delta l \to 0}
\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta l}
= \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\|
= \kappa
\quad\text{(curvature)}
\]
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l): \ \text{curvature vector}
\qquad
\kappa = \|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\|: \ \text{curvature}
\]
\[
\mathbf{T}(l) = \tilde{\mathbf{x}}'(l): \ \text{unit tangent vector of the curve}
\]
\[
\mathbf{N}(l) =
\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}''(l)\|}:
\ \text{(unit) principal normal vector of the curve}
\]
\[
\mathbf{T}'(l) = \kappa \mathbf{N}(l)
\]
\[
0 = \langle \mathbf{N}(l), \mathbf{N}(l) \rangle'
= 2\langle \mathbf{N}(l), \mathbf{\dot{N}}(l) \rangle
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
\mathbf{\dot{N}}(l) \ \text{is orthogonal to } \mathbf{N}(l)
\]
\[
0 = \langle \mathbf{T}(l), \mathbf{N}(l) \rangle'
= \kappa \langle \mathbf{N}(l), \mathbf{N}(l)\rangle
+ \langle \mathbf{T}(l), \mathbf{\dot{N}}(l) \rangle
= \kappa + \langle \mathbf{T}(l), \mathbf{\dot{N}}(l) \rangle
\]
Fundamental Equations of Plane Curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\):
\[
\dot{\mathbf{N}}(l) = -\kappa \mathbf{T}(l)
\]
In arc-length parametrization, the moving frame \((\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N})\) of a plane curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) satisfies the fundamental equations:
\[
(\mathbf{T} \ \mathbf{N})'
=
(\mathbf{T} \ \mathbf{N})
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & -\kappa \\
\kappa & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Given a curvature function \(\kappa(l)\) and any orthonormal initial vectors \(\mathbf{T}_0, \mathbf{N}_0\), the above system has a unique solution.
The curve is then obtained from
\[
\mathbf{x}(l)
=
\mathbf{x}_0
+
\int_0^l \mathbf{T}(s)\, ds
\]
A plane curve is uniquely determined by its curvature.
Fundamental Equations of Plane Curve in \(\mathbb{R}^3\):
\[
\mathbf{B}(l) = \mathbf{T}(l) \times \mathbf{N}(l):
\ \text{the (unit) binormal vector of the curve}
\]
\(\dot{\mathbf{N}}(l)\) is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{N}(l)\)
\[
\langle \mathbf{T}(l), \dot{\mathbf{N}}(l) \rangle = -\kappa
\]
\[
\dot{\mathbf{N}}(l)
= -\kappa \mathbf{T}(l) + \tau \mathbf{B}(l)
\]
\[
\tau = \langle \dot{\mathbf{N}}(l), \mathbf{B}(l) \rangle
\quad
\text{(torsion of the curve)}
\]
\[
\dot{\mathbf{B}}(l)
= \dot{\mathbf{T}}(l) \times \mathbf{N}(l)
+ \mathbf{T}(l) \times \dot{\mathbf{N}}(l)
= \tau\, \mathbf{T}(l) \times \mathbf{B}(l)
= -\tau\, \mathbf{N}(l)
\]
In arc-length parametrization, the moving frame \((\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B})\) of a space curve in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) satisfies:
\[
(\mathbf{T}\ \mathbf{N}\ \mathbf{B})'
=
(\mathbf{T}\ \mathbf{N}\ \mathbf{B})
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & -\kappa & 0 \\
\kappa & 0 & -\tau \\
0 & \tau & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
A space curve in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is uniquely determined by its curvature and torsion.
Frenet–Serret Formulas:
\[
\mathbf{T}
= \frac{\mathbf{x}'}{\|\mathbf{x}'\|}
\]
\[
\frac{dt}{dl} = \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}'\|}
\]
\[
\mathbf{T}'
= \frac{\mathbf{x}''}{\|\mathbf{x}'\|}
- \frac{\mathbf{x}'}{\|\mathbf{x}'\|^{3}}
\langle \mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}'' \rangle
= \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}'\|}
\left( \mathbf{x}'' - \mathbf{T}\langle \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{x}'' \rangle \right)
\]
\[
\dot{\mathbf{T}}
= \mathbf{T}'\frac{dt}{dl}
\quad\text{(curvature vector)}
\]
\[
\kappa
= \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}'\|^{2}}
\left\|\mathbf{x}'' - \mathbf{T}\langle\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{x}''\rangle\right\|
\]
\[
\mathbf{N}
= \frac{\dot{\mathbf{T}}}{\|\dot{\mathbf{T}}\|}
= \frac{\mathbf{x}'' - \mathbf{T}\langle \mathbf{T},\mathbf{x}''\rangle}
{\left\|\mathbf{x}'' - \mathbf{T}\langle \mathbf{T},\mathbf{x}''\rangle\right\|}
\]
\[
\mathbf{B}
= \frac{\mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}''}{\|\mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}''\|}
\]
\[
\mathbf{B}'
=
\frac{\mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}''' - \mathbf{B}
\langle \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}''' \rangle}
{\|\mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}''\|}
\]
\[
\dot{\mathbf{B}}
=
\mathbf{B}'\frac{dt}{dl}
=
- \tau \mathbf{N}
\]
\[
\tau
= -\langle \dot{\mathbf{B}}, \mathbf{N} \rangle
\]
\[
\tau
=
\frac{\langle \mathbf{x}''',\mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N}\rangle}
{\|\mathbf{x}'\times\mathbf{x}''\|}
=
\frac{\langle\mathbf{x}''',\mathbf{B}\rangle}
{\|\mathbf{x}'\times\mathbf{x}''\|}
=
\frac{\langle \mathbf{x}''', \mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}'' \rangle}
{\|\mathbf{x}' \times \mathbf{x}''\|^{2}}
\]

title: Series of Functions and Power Series
text:
TipUniform and Pointwise Convergence





Let \(I \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\), for a function \(f : I \to \mathbb{R}\), we denote:
\[
\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{\mathbf{x} \in I} |f(\mathbf{x})|.
\]
For a sequence of functions \(f_n : I \to \mathbb{R}\), we say that \(f_n\) uniformly converges to \(f\) on \(I\) (denoted as \(f_n \overset{I}{\rightrightarrows} f\)), if:
\[
\lim_{n \to +\infty} \|f_n - f\|_\infty = 0,
\]
That is: for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an \(N(\varepsilon)\) such that for any positive integer \(n > N(\varepsilon)\) and for any \(\mathbf{x} \in I\), \(|f_n(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x})| < \varepsilon\). Here, “uniform” means that \(N(\varepsilon)\) is independent of \(\mathbf{x} \in I\).
If for any \(\mathbf{x} \in I\), we have \(\lim_{n \to +\infty} f_n(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x})\), then \(f_n\) is said to pointwise converge to \(f\) on \(I\), which means for any \(\mathbf{x} \in I\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an \(N(\mathbf{x}, \varepsilon)\) such that for any positive integer \(n > N(\mathbf{x}, \varepsilon)\), \(|f_n(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x})| < \varepsilon\).
A sequence of functions \(f_n\) is said to converge non-uniformly to \(f\) on \(I\) if \(f_n\) converges pointwise to \(f\) on \(I\), but does not converge uniformly to \(f\).

TipMultivariate Function





An \(m\)-variable function is a mapping \(f : D \to \mathbb{R}\), where \(D\) is \(\mathbb{R}^m\) or a subset of it, and the function value \(y\) and independent variables \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m\) satisfy \(y = f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m)\).

section: 1.2 Distance and Limits of Sequences in \(\mathbb{R}^m\)
text:
1.2 Distance and Limits of Sequences in \(\mathbb{R}^m\)






TipDistance on \(\mathbb{R}^m\)





A bivariate function \(d : \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}\) is called a distance on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) if it satisfies:

For any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = d(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) \ge 0\);
For any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = 0\) if and only if \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}\);
For any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) \le d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) + d(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z})\).


For \(r > 0\), denote \[
  B(\mathbf{x}, r) := \{\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m \mid d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) < r\},
  \] which is called the open ball centered at \(\mathbf{x}\) with radius \(r\).
A distance \(d\) on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is said to be translation-invariant if for any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^m\),

\[
d(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z}) = d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}).
\]









TipNorm on \(\mathbb{R}^m\)





A function \(\|\cdot\| : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}\) is called a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) if it satisfies: 1. For any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(\|\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\| \le \|\mathbf{x}\| + \|\mathbf{y}\|\); 2. For any \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(\|\mathbf{x}\| \ge 0\); \(\|\mathbf{x}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\); 3. For any \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) and any \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\|\lambda \mathbf{x}\| = |\lambda| \|\mathbf{x}\|\).









TipMatrix Norm





Given a norm \(\|\cdot\|\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and a square matrix \(A\) of order \(n\), the matrix norm of \(A\) is defined as: \[
\begin{aligned}
\|A\| = \max_{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1} \|A\mathbf{v}\|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Also \[
\begin{aligned}
\|A\| = \max_{\mathbf{v}\neq 0} \frac{\|A\mathbf{v}\|}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}.
\end{aligned}
\]




Theorem 1.1  

For any matrix \(A\), the norm is always non-negative, and it is zero if and only if the matrix itself is the zero matrix.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|A\| \geq 0, \quad \text{and} \quad \|A\| = 0 \iff A = \mathbf{0}
\end{aligned}
\]

Multiplying a matrix by a scalar \(\alpha\) scales the norm by the absolute value of that scalar.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\alpha A\| = |\alpha| \cdot \|A\|
\end{aligned}
\]

The norm of the sum of two matrices is less than or equal to the sum of their individual norms.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|A + B\| \leq \|A\| + \|B\|
\end{aligned}
\]

For induced norms, the norm of a product of matrices is bounded by the product of their norms.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|AB\| \leq \|A\| \cdot \|B\|
\end{aligned}
\]

By the very definition of the induced norm, the transformation of any vector \(\mathbf{v}\) by matrix \(A\) is bounded by the matrix norm:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|A\mathbf{v}\| \leq \|A\| \cdot \|\mathbf{v}\|
\end{aligned}
\]







TipInner Product on \(\mathbb{R}^m\)





A bivariate function \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}\) is called an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) if it satisfies: 1. For any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x} \rangle\); 2. For any \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) and any \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\), \[
   \langle \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z} \rangle + \beta \langle \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \rangle;
   \] 3. For any \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x} \rangle \ge 0\); and \(\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x} \rangle = 0\) if and only if \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\).









TipDefinition





For any \(p \ge 1\), \[
\|\mathbf{x}\|_p := (|x^1|^p + \dots + |x^m|^p)^{\frac{1}{p}}
\] defines a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) ,which induces a distance on \(\mathbb{R}^m\): \[
d_p(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) := (|x^1 - y^1|^p + \dots + |x^m - y^m|^p)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
\]




Theorem 1.2  

\(\|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty := \max\{|x^1|, \dots, |x^m|\}\).
\(\|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty \le \|\mathbf{x}\|_p \le m^{\frac{1}{p}} \|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty\).
\(\frac{1}{m^{\frac{1}{q}}} \|\mathbf{x}\|_q \le \|\mathbf{x}\|_p \le m^{\frac{1}{p}} \|\mathbf{x}\|_q\).



Corollary 1.1 Any norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is equivalent to the norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\),







TipLimits of Sequences in \(\mathbb{R}^m\)





Let \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) be a sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). 1. The sequence \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) is said to be bounded if there exists \(M > 0\) such that for any positive integer \(n\), \(\|\mathbf{x}_n\| \le M\).

The sequence \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) is said to be convergent if there exists \(A \in \mathbb{R}^m\) such that for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a positive integer \(N(\varepsilon) > 0\) such that for any positive integer \(n\), whenever \(n \ge N(\varepsilon)\), we have \(\|\mathbf{x}_n - A\| < \varepsilon\). Such an \(A\) is called a limit of the sequence \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\). We denote \(A = \lim\limits_{n \to +\infty} \mathbf{x}_n\).
The sequence \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) is said to be a Cauchy sequence if for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a positive integer \(N(\varepsilon) > 0\) such that for any positive integers \(p, q\), whenever \(p, q \ge N(\varepsilon)\), we have \(\|\mathbf{x}_p - \mathbf{x}_q\| < \varepsilon\).





Theorem 1.3 Let \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}\) be a sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), where \(\mathbf{x}_n = (x_n^1, \dots, x_n^m)^T\). Then:

\(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) is a bounded sequence if and only if for any \(1 \le k \le m\), the sequence \(\{x_n^k\}_{n \ge 1}\) is a bounded sequence.
\(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) is a Cauchy sequence if and only if for any \(1 \le k \le m\), the sequence \(\{x_n^k\}_{n \ge 1}\) is a Cauchy sequence.
\(\lim\limits_{n \to +\infty} \mathbf{x}_n = A\) if and only if for any \(1 \le k \le m\), \(\lim\limits_{n \to +\infty} x_n^k = A_k\).



Theorem 1.4  

A sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is convergent if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
Any bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) has a convergent subsequence.








TipClosed Set





A set \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\) is said to be a closed set if: for any sequence \(\{\mathbf{x}_n\}_{n \ge 1}\) in \(E\), if the sequence has a limit \(\lim\limits_{n \to +\infty} \mathbf{x}_n\), then this limit is also in \(E\).

title: Series
text:
TipSeries





Given a sequence \(\{a_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\) in a linear space \(V\), the expression \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots\) is called a series, and \(a_n\) is called the \(n\)-th term of this series. For a positive integer \(N\), \(\sum_{k=1}^N a_k = a_1 + \cdots + a_N\) is called the \(N\)-th partial sum of the series, denoted as \(S_N\).
If there exists an \(S \in V\) such that \(\lim_{N \to +\infty} S_N = S\), then the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) is said to be convergent, and \(S\) is called the sum of the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\), denoted as \(S = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\).
Here, the meaning of \(\lim_{N \to +\infty} S_N = S\) is: for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an \(N(\varepsilon)\) such that for any positive integer \(N > N(\varepsilon)\), we have \(\|S_N - S\| < \varepsilon\). Where \(\|\cdot\|\) is the norm in \(V\).
A series that does not converge is called a divergent series.

title: Series
text:
8.1 Absolute Convergence and Comparison Tests






TipAbsolute Convergence





A series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots\) is said to converge absolutely if the series of norms:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|a_k\|
\]
converges.









NoteProposition






An absolutely convergent series is convergent.
Suppose \(a_k = O(b_k)\) as \(k \to +\infty\), that is, there exist \(K_0\) and \(M > 0\) such that \(\|a_k\| \le M\|b_k\|\) for all \(k \ge K_0\).


If \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|b_k\|\) converges, then \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|a_k\|\) converges.
If \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|a_k\|\) diverges, then \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|b_k\|\) diverges.





Theorem 8.2 (Integral Test) Let \(f: (0, +\infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-negative, monotonically decreasing function. Then the improper integral:
\[
\int_1^{+\infty} f(x) \, \mathrm{d}x
\]
converges if and only if the series:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty f(k)
\]
converges.


Theorem 8.3 (D’Alembert’s Ratio Test) Let \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) be a series in a complete normed linear space, and suppose \(a_k \neq 0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Let:
\[
R = \limsup_{k \to +\infty} \frac{\|a_{k+1}\|}{\|a_k\|}, \quad \text{and} \quad r = \liminf_{k \to +\infty} \frac{\|a_{k+1}\|}{\|a_k\|}
\]

If \(R < 1\), the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) converges absolutely.
If \(r > 1\), the series diverges.
If \(r \le 1 \le R\), the test is inconclusive.



Theorem 8.4 (Cauchy’s Root Test) Let \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) be a series in a complete normed linear space. Let:
\[
\rho = \limsup_{k \to +\infty} \sqrt[k]{\|a_k\|}
\]

If \(\rho < 1\), the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) converges absolutely.
If \(\rho > 1\) (or \(\rho = +\infty\)), the series diverges.
If \(\rho = 1\), the test is inconclusive.



Theorem 8.5 (Raabe’s Test) Let \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) be a series in a complete normed linear space, and suppose \(a_k \neq 0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Let:
\[
\rho = \lim_{k \to +\infty} k \left( \frac{\|a_k\|}{\|a_{k+1}\|} - 1 \right)
\]

If \(\rho > 1\), the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) converges absolutely.
If \(\rho < 1\), the series of norms \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|a_k\|\) diverges (i.e., the series does not converge absolutely).
If \(\rho = 1\), the test is inconclusive.



Theorem 8.6 (Gauss’s Test) Let \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) be a series in a complete normed linear space, and suppose \(a_k \neq 0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). If the ratio of successive norms can be expressed as an asymptotic expansion of the form:
\[
\frac{\|a_k\|}{\|a_{k+1}\|} = 1 + \frac{\beta}{k} + O\left(\frac{1}{k^p}\right) \quad \text{as } k \to +\infty
\]
where \(\beta\) is a real constant, and \(p > 1\) is a strictly positive constant (the remainder term is bounded by \(C/k^p\)). Then:

If \(\beta > 1\), the series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) converges absolutely.
If \(\beta \le 1\), the series of norms \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|a_k\|\) diverges.

title: Logic
text:
Representation (Syntax): defines a set of valid formulas.
Semantics: for each formula, specify a set of models (assignments / configurations of the world).
Inference rule: a rule that allows us to derive new formulas from existing ones.

title: Logic
text:
2.1 Representation
Formal languages: syntax and model

2.1.1 Propositional logic
Syntax:

Propositional symbols (atomic formulas): \(A, B, C\)
Logical connectives: \(\neg, \land, \lor, \to, \leftrightarrow\)
Build up formulas recursively—if \(f\) and \(g\) are formulas, so are the following:

Negation: \(\neg f\)
Conjunction: \(f \land g\)
Disjunction: \(f \lor g\)
Implication: \(f \to g\)
Biconditional: \(f \leftrightarrow g\)


Model:
A model \(w\) in propositional logic is an assignment of truth values to propositional symbols.
Interpretation function:
Let \(f\) be a formula and \(w\) be a model. An interpretation function \(\mathcal{I}(f,w)\) returns:

true (1) (say that \(w\) satisfies \(f\))
false (0) (say that \(w\) does not satisfy \(f\))

Base case: For a propositional symbol \(p\) (e.g., \(A, B, C\)):
\[
\mathcal{I}(p,w) = w(p)
\]
Recursive case
Let \(\mathcal{M}(f)\) be the set of models \(w\) for which \(\mathcal{I}(f,w) = 1\).
Knowledge base:
A knowledge base \(\mathrm{KB}\) is a set of formulas representing their conjunction / intersection:
\[
\mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) = \bigcap_{f \in \mathrm{KB}} \mathcal{M}(f).
\]


2.1.2 First-order logic
Syntax:

Terms denote objects: constant symbols \(c\), variables \(x\), and function applications \(f(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\), where each \(t_i\) is a term.
Formulas are built from:

Atomic formulas: \(P(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\); also \(t_1=t_2\) in logic with equality.
Connectives applied to formulas: \(\neg,\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\).
Quantifiers applied to formulas: \(\forall x\,\varphi\), \(\exists x\,\varphi\).


Models:

A model \(w\) specifies a nonempty domain \(D\) and interprets:

Constant symbols as objects: \(w(c)\in D\).
Function symbols as functions: \(w(f):D^n\to D\).
Predicate symbols as sets of tuples: \(w(P)\subseteq D^n\), equivalently functions \(D^n\to\{0,1\}\).

A separate variable assignment \(s:\mathrm{Var}\to D\) gives variables their values: \(s(x)\in D\).

For example, if \(w(\mathrm{alice})=o_1\), \(w(\mathrm{arithmetic})=o_3\), and \((o_1,o_3)\in w(\mathrm{Knows})\), then \(\mathrm{Knows}(\mathrm{alice},\mathrm{arithmetic})\) is true.

title: Logic
text:
2.2 Inference

2.2.1 Entailment and satisfiability
Entailment: \(\mathrm{KB}\) entails \(f\) (written \(\mathrm{KB} \models f\)) iff \(\mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) \subseteq \mathcal{M}(f)\).
Contradiction: \(\mathrm{KB}\) contradicts \(f\) iff \(\mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) \cap \mathcal{M}(f) = \emptyset\).
Contingency:
\[
\emptyset \subsetneq \mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) \cap \mathcal{M}(f) \subsetneq \mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB})
\]
Satisfiability: A knowledge base \(\mathrm{KB}\) is satisfiable if \(\mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) \neq \emptyset\).


2.2.2 SAT and model-checking
Model checking:

Input: knowledge base \(\mathrm{KB}\)
Output: exists satisfying model (\(\mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) \neq \emptyset\))?

Popular algorithms:

DPLL (backtracking + propagation + pruning)
WalkSat (randomized local search over complete assignments)



2.2.3 Inference rules
Modus ponens inference rule:
For any propositional symbols \(p\) and \(q\):
\[
\frac{p,\quad p \to q}{q}
\]
General inference rule:
If \(f_1, \ldots, f_k, g\) are formulas, then the following is an inference rule:
\[
\frac{f_1,\quad \ldots,\quad f_k}{g}
\]
Algorithm: forward inference:
Input: set of inference rules \(\mathrm{Rules}\).
Repeat until no changes to \(\mathrm{KB}\):

Choose set of formulas \(f_1, \ldots, f_k \in \mathrm{KB}\).
If matching rule \(\frac{f_1,\quad \cdots,\quad f_k}{g}\) exists, add \(g\) to \(\mathrm{KB}\).

Derivation:
\(\mathrm{KB}\) derives/proves \(f\) (\(\mathrm{KB} \vdash f\)) iff \(f\) eventually gets added to \(\mathrm{KB}\).


2.2.4 Horn clauses and modus ponens
Propositional logic:
Definite clause: A definite clause has the following form:
\[
(p_1 \land \cdots \land p_k) \to q
\]
where \(p_1, \ldots, p_k, q\) are propositional symbols.
Horn clause: A Horn clause is either:

a definite clause \((p_1 \land \cdots \land p_k \to q)\)
a goal clause \((p_1 \land \cdots \land p_k \to \mathrm{false})\)

Modus ponens:
\[
\frac{p_1,\quad \cdots,\quad p_k,\quad (p_1 \land \cdots \land p_k) \to q}{q}
\]
First-order logic:
Definite clause: A definite clause has the following form:
\[
\forall x_1 \cdots \forall x_n \bigl((a_1 \land \cdots \land a_k) \to b\bigr)
\]
for variables \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) and atomic formulas \(a_1, \ldots, a_k, b\) (which contain those variables).
Modus ponens:
\[
\frac{a_1,\ldots,a_k \qquad \forall x_1\cdots\forall x_n\bigl((a_1\land\cdots\land a_k)\to b\bigr)}{b}
\]
Substitution:
A substitution \(\theta\) is a mapping from variables to terms.
\(\operatorname{Subst}[\theta, f]\) returns the result of performing substitution \(\theta\) on \(f\).
Unification:
Unification takes two formulas \(f\) and \(g\) and returns a substitution \(\theta\) which is the most general unifier:
\[
\operatorname{Unify}[f,g] = \theta
\quad \text{such that} \quad
\operatorname{Subst}[\theta,f] = \operatorname{Subst}[\theta,g]
\]
or “fail” if no such \(\theta\) exists.


2.2.5 Complexity
Theorem: completeness:
Modus ponens is complete for first-order logic with only Horn clauses.
Theorem: semi-decidability:
First-order logic (even restricted to only Horn clauses) is semi-decidable.

If \(\mathrm{KB} \models f\), forward inference on complete inference rules will prove \(f\) in finite time.
If \(\mathrm{KB} \not\models f\), no algorithm can show this in finite time.



2.2.6 Resolution
Propositional resolution rule:
\[
\frac{f_1 \lor \cdots \lor f_n \lor p,\quad \neg p \lor g_1 \lor \cdots \lor g_m}
{f_1 \lor \cdots \lor f_n \lor g_1 \lor \cdots \lor g_m}
\]
Conjunctive normal form (CNF):
A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses.
Proposition: conversion to CNF:
Every formula \(f\) in propositional logic can be converted into an equivalent CNF formula \(f'\):
\[
\mathcal{M}(f) = \mathcal{M}(f')
\]
First-order conversion to CNF:

All variable have universal quantifiers by default
Introduce Skolem functions (e.g., \(Y(x)\)) to represent existentially quantified variables.

First-order resolution rule:
\[
\frac{
f_1 \lor \cdots \lor f_n \lor p,\qquad
\neg q \lor g_1 \lor \cdots \lor g_m
}{
\operatorname{Subst}[\theta,\,
f_1 \lor \cdots \lor f_n \lor g_1 \lor \cdots \lor g_m]
}
\]
where \(\theta = \operatorname{Unify}[p,q]\).

title: Logic
text:
2.3 Semantics

2.3.1 Desiderata for inference rules
Semantics:
Interpretation defines entailed/true formulas: \(\mathrm{KB} \models f\).
\[
\mathcal{M}(\mathrm{KB}) \subseteq \mathcal{M}(f)
\]
Syntax:
Inference rules derive formulas: \(\mathrm{KB} \vdash f\)


2.3.2 Soundness
A set of inference rules \(\mathrm{Rules}\) is sound if:
\[
\{f : \mathrm{KB} \vdash f\}
\subseteq
\{f : \mathrm{KB} \models f\}.
\]


2.3.3 Completeness
A set of inference rules \(\mathrm{Rules}\) is complete if:
\[
\{f : \mathrm{KB} \vdash f\} \supseteq \{f : \mathrm{KB} \models f\}
\]


2.3.4 Fixing completeness

Option 1: Restrict the allowed set of formulas
propositional logic \(\to\) propositional logic with only Horn clauses
Option 2: Use more powerful inference rules
Modus ponens \(\to\) resolution



2.3.5 Theorem: Modus ponens on Horn clauses
Modus ponens is complete with respect to Horn clauses:

Suppose \(\mathrm{KB}\) contains only Horn clauses and \(p\) is an entailed propositional symbol.
Then applying modus ponens will derive \(p\).

title: Transformations
text:
2.2 Rotation
Topology: Structural properties of a manifold.
Two surfaces \(M\) and \(N\) are topologically equivalent if there is a differentiable bijection between \(M\) and \(N\).
Orientation: Space frame and body frame.
The Set of Rotations: The special orthogonal group is
\[
SO(n) = \{R \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n} : \det(R)=1,\ RR^T=I\}.
\]
The topology of \(SO(2)\) and \(SO(3)\) is different from \((-1,1)^n\), so parameterizing rotations in networks is tricky.

title: Transformations
text:
2.3 3D Rotation Representations

2.3.1 Euler Angles
\[
R_x(\alpha)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\
0 & \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
R_y(\beta)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\beta & 0 & \sin\beta \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
-\sin\beta & 0 & \cos\beta
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
R_z(\gamma)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\gamma & -\sin\gamma & 0 \\
\sin\gamma & \cos\gamma & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
For an arbitrary rotation,
\[
R = R_z(\gamma)R_y(\beta)R_x(\alpha).
\]
Euler Angle is not unique for some rotations (gimbal lock).


2.3.2 Axis-Angle
Euler’s Rotation Theorem:

Any rotation in \(SO(3)\) is equivalent to rotation about a fixed axis \(\omega \in \mathbb{R}^3\) through a positive angle \(\theta\).
\(\hat{\omega}\): unit vector of rotation axis \((\|\hat{\omega}\| = 1)\).
\(\theta\): angle of rotation.
\(R \in SO(3) := \operatorname{Rot}(\hat{\omega}, \theta)\).

Skew-Symmetric Matrix:

\(A\) is skew-symmetric if
\[
A = -A^T.
\]
Skew-symmetric matrix operator:
\[
\omega =
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_1 \\
\omega_2 \\
\omega_3
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
[\omega]
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & -\omega_3 & \omega_2 \\
\omega_3 & 0 & -\omega_1 \\
-\omega_2 & \omega_1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Cross product can be represented as a linear transformation:
\[
a \times b = [a]b.
\]

Rodrigues Formula:

Can prove that
\[
  [\hat{\omega}]^3 = -[\hat{\omega}].
  \]

Then, use Taylor expansion of \(\sin\) and \(\cos\):
\[
e^{[\hat{\omega}]\theta}
=
I
+
[\hat{\omega}]\sin\theta
+
[\hat{\omega}]^2(1-\cos\theta).
\]
Recover Axis-Angle from Rotation Matrix:

For \(0 < \theta < \pi\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta &= \arccos\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}(R)-1}{2}\right), \\
[\hat{\omega}] &= \frac{R-R^T}{2\sin\theta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
When \(\theta=0\), \(R=I\). There is no actual rotation, so the rotation axis \(\hat{\omega}\) can be arbitrary.
When \(\theta=\pi\), \((\hat{\omega},\pi)\) and \((-\hat{\omega},\pi)\) represent the same rotation.



2.3.3 Quaternion
Mathematical Definition:
Quaternion is a more generalized complex number:
\[
q = w + xi + yj + zk
\]

\(w\) is the real part and \(\vec{v} = (x,y,z)\) is the imaginary part.
Imaginary units satisfy
\[
i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1
\]
They are anti-commutative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
ij &= k = -ji, \\
jk &= i = -kj, \\
ki &= j = -ik.
\end{aligned}
\]

Properties of General Quaternions:

In vector form, the product of two quaternions:
For \(q_1 = (w_1, \vec{v}_1)\) and \(q_2 = (w_2, \vec{v}_2)\),
\[
q_1 q_2
=
\left(
w_1 w_2 - \vec{v}_1^{\,T}\vec{v}_2,\;
w_1 \vec{v}_2 + w_2 \vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_1 \times \vec{v}_2
\right).
\]
Conjugate, norm, and inverse:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^* &= (w, -\vec{v}), \\
\|q\|^2 &= w^2 + \vec{v}^{\,T}\vec{v} = qq^* = q^*q, \\
q^{-1} &:= \frac{q^*}{\|q\|^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Unit Quaternion as Rotation:

Rotate a vector \(\vec{x}\) by quaternion \(q\):

Augment \(\vec{x}\) to
\[
x = (0, \vec{x})
\]
Rotate by
\[
x' = qxq^{-1}
\]

Compose rotations by quaternion:

First rotate by \(q_1\) and then by \(q_2\):
\[
q_2(q_1xq_1^*)q_2^*
\]
Since
\[
q_2(q_1xq_1^*)q_2^*
=
(q_2q_1)x(q_1^*q_2^*),
\]
and
\[
(q_2q_1)^*
=
q_1^*q_2^*,
\]
we conclude that composing rotations is as simple as multiplying quaternions:
\[
q_{\text{total}} = q_2q_1.
\]


Conversion between Quaternions and Axis-Angle:

Given the rotation axis \(\hat{\omega}\) and rotation angle \(\theta\),
\[
q
=
\left[
\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right),
\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\hat{\omega}
\right].
\]
Quaternion is very close to the angle-axis representation.
For a unit quaternion \(q=(w,\vec{v})\), the rotation angle is
\[
\theta
=
2\arccos(w).
\]
The rotation axis is
\[
\hat{\omega}
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{\sin(\theta/2)}\vec{v},
& \theta\neq 0, \\[8pt]
0,
& \theta=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Learning Perspective:
Each rotation corresponds to two quaternions. Networks need to normalize quaternions to unit length, which may cause large or small gradients in practice.

title: Transformations
text:
2.4 Viewing Transformation
The standard graphics transformation pipeline is
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{\text{object}} &\xrightarrow{M} p_{\text{world}}
\xrightarrow{V} p_{\text{camera}} \\
p_{\text{camera}} &\xrightarrow{P} p_{\text{canonical}}
\xrightarrow{\text{viewport}} p_{\text{screen}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
where:

\(M\): modeling transformation
\(V\): view / camera transformation
\(P\): projection transformation
viewport: maps canonical coordinates to screen coordinates

The first three transformations are often combined as
\[
p_{\text{clip}}
=
PVM\,p_{\text{object}}.
\]

2.4.1 Projection Transformation

3D to 2D
Orthographic Projection vs. Perspective Projection

Orthographic Projection:

Camera located at origin, looking at -Z, up at Y
Drop Z coordinate
Translate and scale the resulting rectangle to \([-1, 1]^2\)

Translate the center to the origin first, then scale each dimension to length 2.
\[
M_{\text{ortho}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{2}{r-l} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{2}{t-b} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \frac{2}{n-f} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & -\frac{r+l}{2} \\
0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{t+b}{2} \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{n+f}{2} \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Perspective Projection:

Most common in Computer Graphics
Further objects are smaller
Parallel lines not parallel; converge to single point

First “squish” the frustum into a cuboid, then apply orthographic projection.
\[
M_{\mathrm{persp}\to\mathrm{ortho}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
n & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & n & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & n+f & -nf \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
M_{\mathrm{ortho}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{2}{r-l} & 0 & 0 & -\dfrac{r+l}{r-l} \\[6pt]
0 & \dfrac{2}{t-b} & 0 & -\dfrac{t+b}{t-b} \\[6pt]
0 & 0 & -\dfrac{2}{f-n} & -\dfrac{f+n}{f-n} \\[6pt]
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]

Aspect ratio = width / height
Field of view (FOV) = angle of the camera lens = \(2\arctan(\frac{h}{2n})\) where \(h\) is the height of the near plane and \(n\) is the distance from the camera to the near plane.



2.4.2 Viewport Transformation

After MVP (Model-View-Projection) transformation \(\rightarrow\) normalized device coordinate (NDC).
Transform the NDC space \((-1,1)^3\) to the screen space
\[
(s_x,s_x+w_s)\times(s_y,s_y+h_s)\times(f_s,n_s)
\]
\(\rightarrow\) another affine transformation.
Usually set \(s_x,s_y\) to \(0\), treat \(w_s,h_s\) as the screen width and height, and set \(f_s,n_s\) to \(-1,1\) so that the \(z\) coordinates are untouched.
